title: the standing prayer
hook: the standing prayer; "sarbat da bhala" — the good of all
tomorrow: a scripture that is the guru

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sakhis, and the rich man's needle. Your line was what will you take with you? Did you ask it before you bought something? Day nineteen.
screen: `THE SAKHIS — WHAT WILL YOU TAKE WITH YOU?`

segments.voice: Please let my kid be okay. Please let me get the job. Please protect us. When things are hard, a prayer can shrink to the size of a family: mine, ours, our side. Now a room full of Sikhs at the end of a service. Everyone rises to their feet. Palms pressed together. One person leads a prayer that everyone knows, recalling the Gurus and the martyrs, asking for help with this family's wedding or that one's illness. And then, in its very last line, it widens out, past the room, past the community, to everyone. Today, the standing prayer.
screen: `PLEASE, FOR MY OWN.` → `A ROOM RISES TO ITS FEET.` → `THE LAST LINE WIDENS OUT.`

segments.voice: Ardas. It comes from a Persian word for a petition, a humble request. It's the prayer Sikhs offer standing, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of services, before a journey, at weddings and funerals, at the start of almost anything important. Ardas has a shape. It opens with verses by Guru Gobind Singh remembering the Gurus, one by one, from Nanak on. Then it remembers: the scripture, the five beloved ones of the Khalsa, the Guru's sons, the men and women who suffered and gave their lives for their faith. It's a prayer with a long memory. Then, in the middle, it becomes personal. The one leading it adds the day's particular requests: a new baby, a sick grandmother, a family moving house, thanks for a harvest. So no two Ardas are exactly the same. And then the end, which is always the same. It asks for chardi kala, the ever-rising spirits of day fifteen, and then three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. Not the good of the people in this room. The good of everyone, everywhere. In the plain sense of the words, that includes people who've never heard of the Gurus, and people who've wronged the community. In a prayer that remembers so much suffering, that's a remarkable place to end. All that memory, and the final request is for the well-being of the whole world. Then the congregation calls out together, the same greeting from day two: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. And they sit down.
screen: `ARDAS — A HUMBLE REQUEST, STANDING.` · `A PRAYER WITH A LONG MEMORY.` · `THE DAY'S OWN REQUESTS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA — THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST US.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up. Let your feet settle and your hands come together in front of your chest. First, bring to mind the people closest to you. Then widen it: your street, your town, strangers on the other side of the world. Then widen it again, to someone you find hard to love. Hold all of them together. If you pray, you can say three words from the Ardas: sarbat da bhala. If not, just stand there wishing them well. The bell holds the time.
Ardas. The standing prayer, a humble request that remembers the past and ends asking for the good of all. Nineteenth word.
Your line: for everyone, not just us. Today, wish someone well who isn't on your side: a rival, another team, a stranger in the news. Day nineteen.

screen: `DAY 19 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SCRIPTURE THAT IS THE GURU.`

howItsDone: Sikhs stand with palms joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, while one person leads the Ardas at the end of services and before important events; it closes by asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

myth: the Ardas is exactly the same every time
the opening and closing are fixed, but the middle carries the day's own requests.
the Ardas ends by asking for the good of everyone
sarbat da bhala: not only Sikhs, not only the room.
Sikhs say the Ardas sitting down
it's the standing prayer: the congregation rises, palms joined.

fork.setup: you're closing a prayer that has just remembered centuries of your community's suffering. what do you ask for last?
options: justice against those who caused it.
the good of all, everyone, everywhere.
fork.reveal: the Ardas ends with sarbat da bhala: the good of all. after all that memory, the last request is for the whole world.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: ardas, a petition or humble request; from Persian.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh prayer.
what it means: the standing prayer: it remembers the Gurus and the martyrs, carries the day's requests, and ends with the good of all.

what a scholar hears: the Ardas isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. its opening comes from Guru Gobind Singh, its form grew with the community's history, and its wording is set out in the Sikh code of conduct.

sources.ref: Ardas, as set out in the Sikh Rehat Maryada
Var Sri Bhagauti Ji (opening of the Ardas), attributed to Guru Gobind Singh

notes: No part of the Ardas is quoted except the Punjabi phrase sarbat da bhala; the structure is described, not rewritten. Confirm the description (opening by Guru Gobind Singh from Var Sri Bhagauti Ji; remembrance of the Panj Pyare, sahibzade, martyrs; personal requests; fixed close).
'Including people who've wronged the community' is an interpretation of sarbat; confirm it is fair.
The practice offers the three words 'if you pray' and never requires them.

Editor review (days 19-37 pass): hook no longer opens 'Think about'/'Now picture' or claims prayer for one's own is 'the most natural thing'; fixed 'yesterday's word, chardi kala' (chardi kala was day 15, yesterday was the sakhis); 'hundreds of years' cut; the reading of sarbat tied to the plain sense of the words.
